claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be homogenized as a high-temperature BCC phase at approximately 1200°C.
Slow cooling from the high-temperature BCC state provides sufficient atomic mobility for substantial diffusion.
Diffusion during slow cooling drives a spinodal-like decomposition of the high-temperature BCC phase.
Spinodal-like decomposition produces local compositional inhomogeneities in the alloy.
The local compositional inhomogeneities lower the free-energy barrier for an ordering transformation during subsequent thermal exposure.
Local compositional fluctuations trigger the nucleation and growth of ordered secondary phases during subsequent thermal exposure.
The ordered secondary phase formed in the metastable BCC matrix may be B2-type.
Differences in atomic diffusivities and chemical affinities mediate the development of local compositional fluctuations and ordering.
Rapid quenching freezes in high-temperature chemical disorder and preserves a comparatively uniform BCC state.
Rapid quenching kinetically suppresses subsequent ordering reactions relative to slow cooling.
After aging at 500°C for 24 hours, slowly cooled samples will have a higher volume fraction of ordered secondary phases than rapidly quenched samples.
Enhanced ordering in the slowly cooled and aged samples will produce distinguishable ordering-related diffraction features in XRD or TEM.
Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will retain a disordered BCC phase and form few ordered secondary phases during the specified aging treatment.
Cooling rates below approximately 10 K/s are generally slow enough for the proposed diffusion-mediated mechanism to operate.
At extremely high cooling rates, such as above 10^3 K/s, insufficient atomic mobility invalidates the proposed slow-cooling decomposition mechanism.
At temperatures well above the ordering onset, the energetic landscape favors transformations other than the proposed ordering pathway.
